list.listitem: If the history, physical examination, initial blood counts, and peripheral blood smear (PBS) are consistent with the diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia purpura (ITP) and do not include atypical findings, additional diagnostic work-up is generally not necessary. C
Treatment decisions are influenced by platelet count and degree of bleeding (see ). Therapy is not required for platelet counts of less than 30,000. C
Initial management includes treatment with oral prednisone. Other choices for treatment include high-dose dexamethasone, IVIG, and WinRho. B

Chronic refractory ITP is defined as persistence for more than 3 months, lack of response to splenectomy, and platelet count less than 50,000. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and methylprednisone. C

background.definition: Isolated thrombocytopenia in a patient with no clinically apparent associated conditions or factors that can cause thrombocytopenia.

list.listitem: The incidence is 1 in 20,000 adults; it increases with age and is more common in adult women.
The incidence in children is 3 to 8 per 100,000.
The incidence for both adults and children is likely an underestimate because it is based on symptomatic disease.
Autoimmune disorder.
Includes genetic and acquired factors.
ITP results from both increased immune destruction of platelets and insufficient platelet production.

Thrombopoiesis in ITP is inadequate to offset the increased rate of platelet destruction. Thrombopoietic (TPO) growth factor agonists are monoclonal antibodies activating the TPO receptor. TPO agonists may be able to increase platelet production.
Autoantibodies, usually IgG, are directed against platelet membrane antigens such as GPIIb/IIIa and then cleared by splenic macrophages.

If the history, physical examination, initial blood counts, and PBS are consistent with the diagnosis of ITP and do not include atypical findings, additional diagnostic work-up is generally not necessary. C

Diagnostic criteria based on ITP-associated laboratory findings are useful in the differential diagnosis of ITP. These criteria confer a 98% sensitivity, 79% specificity, 95% positive predictive value, and 90% negative predictive value. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Presents with systemic symptoms and signs; confirmed by viral antibodies
Systemic symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, leukocytosis, anemia
Always associated with other abnormalities in PBS
Elicited from history, examination, and blood work
Actual platelet count is normal but appears low because of clumping on blood smear
Characterized by anemia, neurologic findings, and renal abnormalities

list.listitem: Target the history and physical toward detecting alternative causes of thrombocytopenia.

When taking the history, assess the patient for systemic symptoms including weight loss, headache, fever, and symptoms of autoimmune disorders. Also determine risk factors for HIV and inquire about pregnancy status and transfusion history. Ask about medications and substances associated with thrombocytopenia including: heparin, alcohol, quinine, sulfonamides, and salicylates.
Inquire about family history of thrombocytopenia, bleeding symptoms, and autoimmune disorders.
Determine the type and severity of bleeding and exclude other causes of thrombocytopenia.
Splenomegaly is rare with ITP. Signs of liver disease or lymphadenopathy suggest autoimmune, infectious, or lymphoproliferative processes.
CBC and examination of PBS are essential in making the diagnosis.

CBC: with the exception of thrombocytopenia, the CBC should be normal in ITP unless accounted for by another condition. Platelet clumps suggest pseudothrombocytopenia, which is usually EDTA dependent. Work-up is simply doing CBC in citrate.

PBS: in ITP, platelets are often larger than normal with high mean platelet volume, but usually giant platelets are not seen. Additionally, normal RBC morphology and normal WBC morphology should be present. If the other cell lines in the blood smear are abnormal, a bone marrow biopsy is needed to rule out other causes of thrombocytopenia.

A set of diagnostic criteria that rely on a CBC with platelets, peripheral smear for reticulocyted platelets and other abnormalities, and thrombopoietin level are shown in . They have been validated prospectively in 112 patients and have excellent positive and negative predictive value.

It is helpful to involve a hematologist with cases of presumed ITP as it is a diagnosis of exclusion. The degree of cytopenia and the presence of symptoms would warrant a quicker referral. A management partnership between the hematologist and the primary care physician can be instrumental in coordinating a steroid taper, making decisions regarding changes in therapy, and managing intercurrent problems while on therapy.
Suspect ITP in patients who present with an unexplained abrupt or insidious onset of petechiae and ecchymosis.
The diagnosis of ITP is based on history, physical examination, CBC, and PBS.
PBS should exclude other causes of thrombocytopenia.
The goal of treatment is to prevent bleeding, not necessarily to return platelet count to normal. C
Treatment decisions are influenced by platelet count and degree of bleeding (see ). Therapy is not required for platelet counts of more than 30,000/mm3. C
Initial management includes treatment with oral prednisone. Other choices for treatment include high-dose dexamethasone, IVIG, WinRho, and romiplostim. B

Chronic refractory ITP is defined as persistence for more than 3 months, lack of response to splenectomy, and platelet count less than 50,000/mm3. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and methylprednisone. C
At onset, half of patients present with platelet counts less than 10,000/mm3, usually necessitating treatment.
Patients who present chronically with a platelet count of more than 30,000/mm3 can be safely observed without specific treatment. Most acute ITP is treated, in an effort to raise the platelet count.

Initial therapy can be prednisone or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Prednisone is given orally at a dose of 1.0 to 2.0 mg/kg/d. Response rates range from 50% to 75% and depend on treatment duration and intensity. Lack of response in 4 weeks is considered treatment failure.
Anti-RhD immunoglobulin (anti-D) is also used for both acute and chronic management. The usual dose is 50 mg/kg and increases platelet counts in approximately 80% of children and 70% of adults.

Rilzabrutinib is an oral BTK inhibitor and has been shown to safely increase platelet counts in a small single arm Phase 1/2 trial. At approximately 6 months, 40% of patients had achieved the targetted increase in platelets.

WinRho, Rhophylac: use only in patients who are Rh(D) positive who have not had splenectomy. These are generally recommended for patients refractory to initial treatment with corticosteroids. They have the same efficacy and time to response as IVIG. Side effects are generally mild and include headache, back pain, nausea, and fever.

Rituximab: anti-CD-20 monoclonal antibodies causing depletion of immunoglobulin-producing B cells, leading to reduction in platelet-specific autoantibodies. Response time is weeks to months. Complete or partial remission is achieved in 25% to 50% of patients. Overall, partial (platelets >50,000) or complete (platelets >150,000) responses are achieved in 63% and 43% of patients, respectively. Many complete responses are sustained for more than a year.

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rituximab in 112 adults with ITP who had not previously responded to corticosteroid treatment found no statistical difference in long-term response rates, but longer time to relapse in the rituximab group.

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of romiplostim, a TPO receptor agonist, in 62 children with ITP of more than 6 months' duration and platelet counts <30,000/mm3 found a statistically significant improved durable platelet response (platelet count >50,000/mm3 without rescue drug use in the preceding 4 weeks) in the intervention group with no difference in adverse effects. However, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of TPO agonists, citing improved platelet counts but lack of bleeding and mortality benefits.

A Phase 1/2 trial gave 22 adults with chronic or persistent ITP a monoclonal antibody targetting CD38-positive cells; 14 patients had a sustained response with normal platelet levels > 100,000/mm3 and 7 relapsed after 2-3 months.
Cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil (Cellcept) have shown promise in chronic ITP.

An international, multicenter RCT (N=205) evaluating the neonatal Fc receptor inhibitor efgartigimod to treat adults with chronic or persistent ITP found the treatment effective in improving sustained platelet counts compared to placebo, including among those with treatment-refractory thrombocytopenia.
Splenectomy is considered second-line therapy for ITP. It is indicated in patients who are unresponsive to steroid therapy or relapse upon discontinuation of steroids.
Response occurs within days; two-thirds of patients will achieve complete remission 5 years following splenectomy and will require no further treatment.
Complications include risk of surgery and serious infection. Laparoscopic surgery is associated with less mortality than laparotomy (0.2% vs 1.0%).
Patients undergoing splenectomy should be immunized against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenza type b at least 2 weeks prior to the procedure.

Eradication of Helicobacter pylori may increase the platelet count. One study demonstrated a relationship between H. pylori and thrombocytopenia. However, this relationship is controversial, especially in United States studies, which have not found a link.
Regardless of platelet count, hospitalization is appropriate for severe life-threatening bleeding.
Hospitalization is also appropriate for patients with platelet counts less than 20,000 with significant mucous membrane bleeding.
Spontaneous remissions do occur. C
Mortality is less than 1% and is due to bleeding or infections. Patients with refractory ITP have increased mortality. B
Chronic refractory ITP is defined as persistence for more than 3 months, lack of response to splenectomy, and platelet count less than 50,000. C
Bone marrow biopsies are appropriate in patients older than 60 years due to higher incidence of myelodysplastic syndromes.
Patients older than 65 years are at increased risk of bleeding and subsequent mortality.
ITP is difficult to distinguish from gestational thrombocytopenia (benign thrombocytopenia of pregnancy). ITP may harm the fetus, whereas gestational thrombocytopenia does not.

Preexisting thrombocytopenia prior to pregnancy suggests ITP. Mild thrombocytopenia is generally suggestive of gestational thrombocytopenia, whereas a platelet count of less than 70,000 is typical of ITP.
Platelet counts in women with ITP should be monitored monthly for the first 2 trimesters, then every other week during the third trimester, and weekly as the pregnancy nears term.

Corticosteroids are not considered teratogenic; however, they can worsen gestational diabetes, hypertension, and bone loss. Teratogenic drugs such as danazol and cyclophosphamide should be avoided. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for betamethasone for ITP in pregnancy.
A platelet count of more than 50,000 is considered safe for delivery and epidural.
As in adults, the diagnosis is made on history, physical examination, CBC, and examination of PBS. Maternal and birth history is relevant in examination of infants.
Most children recover completely within a few weeks even without treatment.

Hospitalization is appropriate for life-threatening bleeding regardless of platelet count. Children with a platelet count of more than 30,000 should not be hospitalized and do not require treatment if asymptomatic.
The impetus for treating children is prevention of intracranial hemorrhage, which rarely occurs with a platelet count over 20,000.
Treatment with IVIG in children with primary acute ITP results in a higher proportion of patients achieving a platelet count greater than 20,000 in 48 hours compared with corticosteroids.

feature.caption: Preliminary Diagnostic Criteria Based on Immune Thrombocytopenia Purpura (ITP)-Associated Laboratory Findings.
feature.feature_body: Thrombocytopenia of <100,000 without morphologic evidence for dysplasia in the peripheral blood smear (required). The presence of 3 or more of the following lab values (including at least one of c, d, and f): a. Absence of anemia b. Normal leukocyte count c. Increased anti-GIIb/IIIa antibody, producing B-cell frequency d. Increased platelet-associated anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibody level e. Elevated levels of reticulated platelets f. Normal or slightly increased thrombopoietin levels (<300 pg/mL) The presence of both criteria was 98% sensitive and 79% specific for diagnosis (LR+ 4.7, LR− 0.025) in a group of 112 patients with suspected ITP. Data from Kuwana M, Kurata Y, Fujimura K, et al. Preliminary laboratory based diagnostic criteria for immune thrombocytopenic purpura: evaluation by multi-center prospective study. J Thromb Haemost 2006;4:1936-1943.
